questions.prompt: What makes a LOLBin attack difficult for file-based application allowlisting to catch?
options: The binary itself is legitimate and Microsoft-signed — the malicious part is in how it's invoked, not what file is on disk
Application allowlisting always blocks them by default
questions.explanation: A LOLBin is a completely legitimate, signed binary an allowlist would already trust — detection has to come from behavior (arguments, parent process, network activity), not file identity.

questions.prompt: In the "Squiblydoo" technique, why does the payload never touch disk?
options: regsvr32's /i: flag with scrobj.dll can execute a COM scriptlet fetched directly from a remote URL
The technique only works on read-only file systems
Windows Defender deletes it immediately after download
questions.explanation: regsvr32 /i:<URL> scrobj.dll pulls and executes the scriptlet directly from the URL, with no file ever written to the local disk — exactly why file-based detection misses it.

questions.prompt: Why is certutil.exe making an outbound network connection considered a strong red flag regardless of its specific arguments?
options: certutil is never allowed to run at all in a healthy environment
A certificate management utility has essentially no legitimate reason to reach the internet on its own
certutil can only be run by Domain Admins
Network connections from certutil are always encrypted maliciously
questions.explanation: certutil's legitimate purpose is local certificate management — outbound network activity from it is inherently anomalous, independent of the specific command-line flags used.

questions.prompt: What's the significance of the LOLBAS project referenced in this lesson?
options: It's a Microsoft tool for blocking LOLBin abuse automatically
It's the canonical, community-maintained catalog of LOLBins beyond the five covered here — cited directly in MITRE's own technique references
It's a certification exam covering LOLBin detection
It only covers Linux binaries, not Windows
questions.explanation: LOLBAS (lolbas-project.github.io) is the community reference MITRE ATT&CK itself cites for T1218.010 — the authoritative place to look beyond this lesson's five highlighted binaries.
